title: Trump Says Houthis Asked US to Stay Out as They Seize Red Sea Chokepoint
excerpt: President Trump said Yemen's Houthis asked Washington not to intervene even as the Iran-backed group seized control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — putting a second major energy chokepoint under threat and driving oil above $100 a barrel.
body:
• Standing alongside Ireland's prime minister in Dublin on September 12, President Trump said the Houthis had "called us" to ask Washington not to intervene in Yemen, adding they were letting "most ships" pass through the Red Sea.
  • The remarks came as the Iran-backed Houthis seized the port of Mocha, the coastal town of Dhubab, and strategic Perim Island — positions that put them astride the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint carrying roughly 10-12 percent of global trade.
  • According to Axios reporting confirmed by the White House, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked Trump twice for US strikes on the Houthis; Trump declined direct military action but offered intelligence support.
  • Oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel as a second major chokepoint — after the Strait of Hormuz — came under threat, raising fears of a global recession, according to energy analysts.

President Donald Trump said on September 12 that Yemen's Houthi rebels had contacted his administration asking the United States not to intervene against them, even as the Iran-backed group completed a lightning offensive that put its fighters in control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — the southern gateway to the Red Sea and one of the world's most critical shipping chokepoints.

Standing alongside Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump told reporters: "The Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us. They don't want us to go after them and would much prefer not having us involved." He added that the group was allowing "most ships" to pass through the strait, with only one unnamed country — widely understood to be Saudi Arabia — being blocked. "We'll get that straightened out," he said, predicting that "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy" in the region.

Trump also confirmed that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — whom he described as a "friend" — had asked him for US military help against the Houthis. According to Axios reporting, bin Salman called twice on Thursday requesting American strikes; Trump declined direct intervention but said Washington would help with intelligence.

Context & Background

The Bab al-Mandeb — Arabic for "Gate of Tears" — is an 18-mile-wide strait between Yemen and Djibouti through which every ship entering or leaving the Red Sea must pass. Together with the Suez Canal, it forms the shortest sea route between Asia and Europe. The strait had already grown sharply in importance since the US-Iran war, which began February 28, effectively shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global oil used to flow. Saudi Arabia rerouted millions of barrels of its oil exports through the Red Sea instead.

On September 10, Houthi forces seized the Red Sea port city of Mocha. By the following day, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters the group had reached Perim — also known as Mayyun — the island that splits the strait into two shipping channels. An unnamed Yemeni military official told AFP the Houthis now control the country's entire Red Sea coast, including the Hanish islands and the mainland town of Dhubab.

Separately, drones launched from Iraq damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline on September 10, forcing Riyadh to shut it down the following day — cutting the kingdom's backup route to the Red Sea. Trump told reporters he believed Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack, though he offered no evidence. Saudi Arabia responded with airstrikes on September 11 targeting the airport at the Houthi-controlled port of Mokha.

Impact & Analysis

The threat to a second major chokepoint has jolted energy markets. Global oil prices were on track to close the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May, according to Reuters. Le Monde reported that ships are being forced to turn back and take lengthy detours — the Cape of Good Hope route around Africa adds at least 10 days to the journey — raising fears of higher oil prices and shipping costs at a time when inflation is already elevated in Europe and the United States.

"The Bab al-Mandeb had been a lifeline. Losing that lifeline has been a wake-up call for the (oil) market of how unsustainable the situation now is."

— Richard Bronze, co-founder of Energy Aspects, to CNN

Analysts argue that the Houthi advance opens a dangerous new front in the Middle East conflict and exposes the limits of the US strategy. "The Houthis have shattered Trump's plan," said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. "Just weeks ago, Trump adopted a strategy of squeezing Iran's economy while keeping military conflict at levels too low to squeeze the American economy."

A senior Trump administration official told reporters the US remains focused on ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea "while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges." The Houthis, meanwhile, have warned against outside intervention: a senior Houthi figure said the group was ready to fight on three fronts — Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government, and any foreign power that joins them.

The political scientists at the Anaween Research Center, a Yemen-based public policy think tank, wrote in a September 10 analysis that the Houthi advance is likely intended in part to "create an additional Iranian leverage card in the Red Sea," restricting even more energy trade as Tehran's war with Washington grinds on. Riyadh, for its part, has been building alternatives: in July it announced a 14-state multinational defensive maritime alliance, including Turkiye, Pakistan, Egypt, and Djibouti, reflecting what analysts describe as Saudi recognition that the US security umbrella has contracted.

Diaspora Angle

The crisis carries direct implications for India: Indian-flagged and Indian-crewed vessels are among the heaviest users of the Red Sea route, and tens of thousands of Indian seafarers work on merchant ships transiting these waters. Any sustained disruption to oil flows also lands on Indian consumers, since India imports the overwhelming share of the crude it consumes — making higher freight costs and $100-plus oil a pocketbook issue far beyond the Gulf.

What's Next

Yemeni government forces have said they will attempt a counter-offensive, deploying weapons and aircraft to retake the coastline and the road to Mocha. Whether Saudi airstrikes and that push can dislodge the Houthis — or whether Trump's prediction that "everything will work out" proves right — remains an open question. For now, shippers are voting with their hulls: the uncertain assurances of a rebel group that it will let "most ships" pass have not stopped the detours, the delays, or the climb in oil prices.
